name: Rabindranath Tagore
summary: Tagore, a Bengali poet and educator, opposed British rule over India while rejecting nation-worship, which he called the organized selfishness of a people and a threat to humanity. He held that human relations rest on co-operation and spiritual unity rather than competition and power, favoured village self-help and education through Santiniketan and Sriniketan, and criticized Gandhi's charkha campaign as a blind faith. His recorded positions are mostly about nationalism, empire, race and caste, and education.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: He rejected the methods of the Bengal revolutionary terrorists and wrote Char Adhyay against them, according to Amiya Dev's account.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: He rejects the British claim that two centuries of 'tutelage' justify rule, saying true modernism is independence of thought and not tutelage under European schoolmasters.

class-collaboration.rationale: In the charkha essay he holds that poverty lay in the separation and wealth in the union of man and man, and Sen reports he criticized class-hatred and revengefulness in Soviet training.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: He describes the British administration of India as a machine that keeps education to the minimum needed to run a foreign government, and condemns nations feeding on others' resources.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: He states that agricultural civilization rests on co-operation and not competition, and that the age of co-ordination is coming; he criticizes unbounded competition between men and nations.

corporate-influence.rationale: In Creative Unity he says the sovereign power of Western peoples is robbed by self-seekers, their opinions fashioned by organised interest and a conspiracy of money and unscrupulous diplomacy.

decide-locally.rationale: The Sriniketan institute he founded worked through village self-help, co-operative societies and panchayats that settle local disputes.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: In his 1925 essay on the charkha he calls isolation from the world's trade the greatest of deprivations and favours co-operation between peoples.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He welcomes the lesson that there is a universal standard of justice to which all men, irrespective of caste and colour, have equal claim, and abhorred untouchability.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He holds India's mission is to unite many races, rejecting both cosmopolitan vagueness and the 'self-idolatry of nation-worship' as the goal of history.

evolved-behavioural-sex-differences.rationale: He writes of a difference inherent in the respective natures of men and women, biological and psychological, as well as inequalities fostered by circumstances.

land-redistribution.rationale: In Letters from Russia he wrote that the right to the land belongs morally to the peasant and not to the landlord.

means-match-ends.rationale: In Letters from Russia he wrote that those without patience to wait for human nature believe in persecution, and that the Soviets' violence had no end.

military-superiority.rationale: He rejects the logic of setting machine against machine and nation against nation, and calls the arms race of rival nations a symptom of the Nation's sickness.

nation-first.rationale: In the 1917 Nationalism lectures he calls the Nation the organized self-interest of a whole people and urges Japan and India never to adopt that selfishness as a religion.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Sadhana says earth, water and fruits are not merely phenomena to be used and left aside, but to be related to in sympathy and not only for material advantage.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Sen reports that he opposed communal sectarianism as a source of discontent and held that the idea of India works against cultural separatism.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: In Creative Unity's essay 'Woman and Home' he writes of the unequal freedom between the sexes, and calls many laws on the relation of man and woman relics of a barbaric age of exclusive possession, kept up by woman's economic helplessness.

patriotic-education.rationale: He denounces teaching children pride in conquest, war trophies and flags to breed contempt for others, and urges Indians to fight the education that puts the country above humanity's ideals.

person-over-state.rationale: He argues that goodness is the purpose of man while success is the aim of the machine, and that the national organization reduces the personal man to a phantom.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: He turns the question of caste back on America ('What have you done with the Red Indian and the Negro?') and condemns its violent methods of keeping aloof from other races.

restore-past-order.rationale: Sen reports that he opposed a romantic overattachment to the past while also rejecting imitation of the West.

sacred-nation.rationale: He describes nation-worship as 'self-idolatry' and 'idolatry of the Nation', and says he has outgrown the teaching that it is almost better than reverence for God and humanity.

self-interest-moral.rationale: He says the ideal of the social man is unselfishness and condemns the nation's organized selfishness; self-interest as a moral good is the opposite of what he teaches.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Sadhana presents spiritual realisation of unity as man's end, and Nationalism calls it an evil day when politics and commerce prevail at the cost of the higher social life.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He criticized Soviet repression in Letters from Russia, warning that terror kills freedom of mind, and held freedom of mind central.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He condemns the Western 'political civilization' that feeds on other peoples' resources and swallows continents, and calls this greed 'patriotism'.

total-state.rationale: In Letters from Russia he objected that the Soviets had erased the line between individual and society, behaving not unlike the Fascists.

universal-morality.rationale: He holds there is a moral law of humanity that applies to individuals and to nations alike, and a universal standard of justice for all men.

war-builds-character.rationale: He argues that organized national power and its wars lead to moral degeneracy and call this the war of retribution of the Nation, rather than any strengthening of character.

notes: Tagore had no office, so there is little record; positions come from his lectures and essays. Searched: nationalism, war and arms, empire and tutelage, race and caste, religion, education, economy and trade, cooperatives and village self-government, Gandhi's charkha and non-cooperation, Soviet Russia (Letters from Russia and Crisis in Civilization read only through secondary quotation), women, technology, ecology. Government, liberty, and most economy statements have no stated position found. Hindu-Muslim and women's questions rest only on a secondary account. Date: positions are mature (1917-1941).
